The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Avraham ben David Yitzchaki
This survey sketches the multidimensional portrait of the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Avraham ben David Yitzchaki, a key figure in the leadership of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel at the beginning of the 18th century. The text examines his glorious lineage and his ties with the sages of his generation, with emphasis on his consistent and international war against the Sabbatean movement and its representative Nehemiah Hayun. The author analyzes his public activity as a shadar and as a spiritual leader who had to contend with economic oppression and persecution by the Ottoman authorities, factors that ultimately led to his surprising retirement from office. In conclusion, the source presents his original halakhic teaching in his book "Zera Avraham," which combines decisive rulings in the areas of marriage and modesty with social sensitivity and legal complexity in monetary law.
The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Avraham ben David Yitzchaki
His Life, Lineage and Network of Family and Torah Ties
Rabbi Avraham ben David Yitzchaki was born in the year 5421 (1661) in Jerusalem, although there are isolated historical opinions holding that his birthplace was the city of Hebron [cite: 1, 2]. He grew up amid the leading rabbinic and kabbalistic leadership of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel at the end of the seventeenth century. His father, Rabbi David Yitzchaki, served as the chief rabbi of Jerusalem, and on his mother's side Rabbi Avraham was a scion of a glorious kabbalistic dynasty, being the grandson of the monumental kabbalist Rabbi Avraham Azulai, author of the book "Chesed le-Avraham" [cite: 1, 2, 3]. These family ties not only paved his path in the world of learning, but also connected him in later generations to a broad chain of Jerusalem leadership; his daughter married Rabbi Raphael Yitzchak Zerachia Azulai, and thus Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki became the grandfather of the Chida (Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai) [cite: 1]. In his leading bibliographical work "Shem ha-Gedolim," the Chida frequently mentions his forebear by a title full of reverence: "our teacher, the great rabbi, our kinsman, Mahara Yitzchaki" [cite: 4, 5].
In his youth Rabbi Avraham was educated in the central yeshivot of Jerusalem, foremost among them the yeshiva "Beit Ya'akov Vega" [cite: 1, 2, 3]. He acquired his Torah from the great men of that generation, foremost among them the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Moshe Galante (the second) and Rabbi Yisrael Ya'akov Hagiz [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Alongside the study of the revealed Torah and halakha, he delved deeply into the study of the hidden wisdom and the teaching of Kabbalah, which he studied together with Rabbi Yosef Bialer, the maternal grandfather of the Chida [cite: 1]. His fellow students were prominent decisors and leaders who deeply influenced the world of halakha, among them Rabbi Chizkiyah da Silva, author of the monumental halakhic work "Pri Chadash," and Rabbi Moshe Hayun [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's network of family and Torah ties was also tightened through his marriage; his father-in-law was his cousin and in-law, Rabbi Avraham Yisrael Ze'evi, who served as the chief rabbi of Hebron [cite: 1]. Rabbi Ze'evi himself was the son-in-law of Rabbi Avraham Conque, author of the book of homilies "Avak Derakhim," which points to close and intricate ties among the elite families of the sages of the Land of Israel at that time [cite: 6]. These ties laid a broad foundation that made Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki a central axis of the public and Torah leadership in the years that followed.
His Public Activity and Statesmanlike Leadership as Rishon LeZion
Upon completing his studies, Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki was appointed to head a large yeshiva in Jerusalem and raised prominent disciples who shaped the face of the Torah world in the next generation [cite: 1, 2]. Among his disciples were Rabbi Yitzchak HaKohen Rapaport, Rabbi Moshe Hagiz (who was also his son-in-law and his great supporter in the public struggles), Rabbi Yitzchak Zerachia Azulai, Rabbi Yisrael Meir Mizrachi and Rabbi Moshe Yisrael [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His disciple Rabbi Yitzchak HaKohen Rapaport later moved to the city of Izmir, founded a splendid yeshiva there and served there as a prominent decisor and halakhic authority alongside Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, author of the book "Batei Kenesiyot," before returning to Jerusalem [cite: 3].
In the year 5468 (1709), following a severe economic crisis that threatened the physical existence of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel and led to the accumulation of heavy debts to the local oppressors, Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki went out as a shadar (sheliach de-rabbanan, an emissary of the rabbis) to the communities of Turkey, Italy and Holland [cite: 1, 2, 3]. This journey, originally intended for the financial purposes of raising donations and rescuing the community, quickly became a central axis of his public and ideological activity throughout the Diaspora, and in its course he established his standing as an all-Jewish leader of supreme authority.
Upon Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's return to Jerusalem in the year 5475 (1715), he was chosen to serve as the fourth Rishon LeZion in the line [cite: 1, 2, 3]. He served in this lofty office for about seven years, until his surprising retirement in the year 5482 (1722) [cite: 1, 2, 3]. This retirement was considered an extraordinary and highly exceptional step at the time, since the accepted custom among the holders of this office was to serve in it until the day of their death [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Analysis of the historical and legal sources sheds new light on the background of his retirement and on the circumstances of his life in that period. An Ottoman legal document from 1725 describes how already in 1718, in the midst of his official tenure as Rishon LeZion, Rabbi Avraham was forced to flee Jerusalem temporarily and find refuge in Hebron, because of severe acts of exploitation, injustice and extortion by the local Ottoman governors and men of power in Jerusalem [cite: 7]. This datum reveals that the economic and personal pressure exerted by the local rulers on the leadership of the Jewish community was unbearable, and severely impaired Rabbi Avraham's ability to manage public affairs from Jerusalem. The flight to Hebron and the prolonged political pressures were, in all likelihood, the main factor that led to his official retirement from the office of Rishon LeZion in the year 5482 (1722), in order to make way for a leadership that could better cope with the debt claims of the authorities at that time [cite: 1, 2, 3, 7].
Rabbi Avraham died in Jerusalem on 13 Sivan 5489 (1729) at the age of about 68, and was buried on the Mount of Olives, in a special plot in the courtyard of the Tomb of Zechariah, in which he was the first deceased to be interred [cite: 1, 2]. His grave and tombstone stood intact until the year 5720 (1960), when the graves and tombstones in this area were removed by a British-Jordanian archaeological expedition during development works carried out in the period of Jordanian rule in East Jerusalem [cite: 1, 2].
The International Campaign against Sabbateanism and the Nehemiah Hayun Controversy
One of the most significant and dramatic chapters in Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's public work is his uncompromising war against the Sabbatean movement, which continued to operate underground and openly in the decades following the apostasy and death of Shabbetai Tzvi [cite: 1, 2, 8]. Rabbi Avraham identified the destructive danger these Sabbatean currents posed to the integrity of halakha and of Jewish tradition, and placed himself at the forefront of the international struggle against the prominent Sabbatean leader Nehemiah Chiya Hayun [cite: 8].
Nehemiah Chiya Hayun, a native of Alexandria who grew up in Jerusalem and Shechem, acted as a continuer of the path of the Sabbatean thinker Avraham Michael Cardozo [cite: 8]. Hayun wandered among various communities, and during his visits to Salonika he laid his hands on the Sabbatean kabbalistic work "Raza de-Meheimanuta," attributed to Shabbetai Tzvi himself [cite: 8]. He changed the name of the book to "Meheimanuta de-Kola" and wrote two distinctly Sabbatean-kabbalistic commentaries on it: "Oz le-Elohim" and "Beit Kodesh ha-Kodashim" [cite: 8]. Hayun tried to spread his teaching under the guise of Orthodox Kabbalah and even succeeded in obtaining by deceit approbations from prominent rabbis in Europe, such as Rabbi David Oppenheim and Rabbi Naftali Katz, who hastened to revoke them as soon as they grasped the true character of the book [cite: 8].
During Hayun's short stay in the Land of Israel, the rabbis of Jerusalem, headed by Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki, identified his heretical and antinomian views and pursued him consistently [cite: 8]. In the year 5468 (1709) Rabbi Avraham issued a sharp letter of condemnation and excommunication (cherem) against Hayun and his books [cite: 1, 8]. When Rabbi Avraham went out on his mission as a shadar in Europe, he turned the fund-raising journey into an ideological campaign to uproot the influence of Sabbateanism in the communities of the Diaspora [cite: 1, 2, 8]. In the year 5470 (1710) he visited Izmir and persuaded the leadership of the community to burn the books of the Sabbateans and denounce them publicly, and a year later, in the year 5471 (1711), he conducted vigorous propaganda in Salonika that led to the complete denunciation of Hayun in that community [cite: 1].
Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's influence went beyond the bounds of his direct activity; he served as a halakhic and leadership engine for his disciples and contemporaries who continued the campaign in Europe [cite: 8]. His son-in-law and disciple, Rabbi Moshe Hagiz, together with the kabbalist Rabbi Yosef Ergas (author of "Shomer Emunim," who expelled Hayun from Livorno) and the rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Amsterdam, Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi (the Chacham Tzvi), led a sharp controversy in Amsterdam against Hayun [cite: 8]. This controversy shook the Jewish community in Amsterdam, since the wealthy Portuguese community, headed by Rabbi Shlomo Ayllon, favored Hayun and saw in the Chacham Tzvi's steps an infringement of its judicial authority [cite: 8]. The bans and polemical books issued against Hayun in that period, such as "Milchamah la-Shem ve-Cherev la-Shem" by Rabbi Moshe Hagiz, relied to a great extent on the halakhic and authoritative backing provided by Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki from the Holy Land [cite: 8].
The immense esteem Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki enjoyed among the sages of Europe found distinct expression in the words of Rabbi Ya'akov Emden (the Ya'avetz), son of the Chacham Tzvi, who met Rabbi Avraham during his visit to Amsterdam and was deeply impressed by his leadership: "A distinguished man, great in Torah and in wisdom, head and shoulders above all the people" [cite: 1]. In this struggle Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki succeeded in halting the spread of early Sabbateanism in Europe, and thereby prevented the collapse of the fences of halakha and tradition in the generation preceding the appearance of the Frankist movement [cite: 8].
His Halakhic Teaching and Torah Writings
Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's Torah teaching was characterized by the fusion of systematic Sephardi-Jerusalem scholarship with comprehensive knowledge of the hidden Torah [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His halakhic work bears the character of striving to clarify the sources of the law from the Gemara and the Rishonim, with a capacity for independent and original decision in places where others refrained from ruling.
His central book of questions and answers, the responsa "Zera Avraham," was printed in two parts after his death [cite: 1, 4, 5, 9, 10]. Its first part was printed in Izmir in the year 5492 (1732), and its second part was printed in Constantinople and Izmir in the year 5494 (1734) at the joint press of Yonah Ashkenazi and David Chazan [cite: 1, 4, 5, 9, 10]. The work is arranged according to the order of the Arba'ah Turim and deals with intricate practical questions addressed to him from all over the Jewish world [cite: 4, 5]. Original volumes of these first printings were found in prestigious bibliographical collections, such as the collection of the Valmadonna Trust and the collection of Ya'akov Chalfon, and over the years were donated to national libraries by scholars such as Avraham Danon [cite: 9, 10].
It should be noted that in a careful bibliographical analysis of the world of the Hebrew book, one must distinguish between the responsa "Zera Avraham" of Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki [cite: 1, 4, 5, 9, 10] and two other works bearing similar titles or identical authors' names:
The book "Zera Avraham" by Rabbi Avraham of the holy community of Glogau: a work that constitutes a commentary on Midrash Rabbah and a commentary on the aggadot of the Jerusalem Talmud [cite: 4, 5, 11]. This commentary on the Midrash was printed several times alongside the books "Yedei Moshe" and "Yefeh Mar'eh" in Amsterdam [cite: 11].
Rabbi Avraham HaKohen Yitzchaki (the second): a famous dayan in the city of Tunis (1789–1864), author of the book "Mishmerot Kehunah," who was active some two generations later and is not connected to the family dynasty of the Jerusalem Rishon LeZion [cite: 12].
Besides the book of responsa, Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki left an extensive body of Torah writing in manuscript, most of which was never printed [cite: 1, 13, 14]. Among the writings that received special mention in the book "Shem ha-Gedolim" are a large and comprehensive work on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah, glosses and explanations on the Tur and Shulchan Arukh Yoreh De'ah, and profound novellae on tractate Gittin and the laws of divorce [cite: 1, 13, 14]. These manuscripts were handed down in his family and were studied in depth by the sages of Jerusalem [cite: 1].
An In-Depth Analysis of His Central Rulings and Methods of Decision
An examination of Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's halakhic method reveals a tendency toward decisive rulings, conservative in the personal and family sphere, but innovative and balancing in the monetary and public sphere. Below is an analysis of five central topics that characterize his halakhic path:
Defining the Prohibition of Seclusion and of Approaching Forbidden Relations as "Be Killed Rather than Transgress"
In the responsa "Zera Avraham" (section Yoreh De'ah, siman 5), Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki presents a stringent and exceptional position regarding the bounds of the prohibition of seclusion (yichud) and of approaching forbidden relations (arayot) [cite: 15, 16]. In his view, which relies on the words of the Baal HaMaor, the stringent law of "be killed rather than transgress" (yehareg ve-al ya'avor) applies to the prohibition of seclusion and even to a light touch [cite: 15, 16]. He reasons that all these distancing measures of modesty are defined as "avizraihu de-gilui arayot" (accessories of forbidden sexual relations), and that they are included directly in the biblical negative commandment forbidding approaching forbidden relations [cite: 15, 16].
This position aroused much controversy among the decisors of later generations, among them the authors of the books "Shem Aryeh" and "Om Ani Chomah," who wondered at Rabbi Avraham's stringency [cite: 15, 16]. They noted that according to the Rambam and the Shulchan Arukh, the essence of the prohibition of seclusion is only from divrei kabbalah (from the words of the scribes) and has no explicit negative commandment from the Torah, and therefore the obligation of self-sacrifice of "be killed rather than transgress" should not be applied to it [cite: 15, 16]. Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki's extreme stringency on this issue is better understood against the background of his uncompromising struggle against Sabbateanism; the Sabbatean movement tended to breach the fences of forbidden relations and modesty under a mystical guise, and Rabbi Avraham's ruling served as a sharp halakhic response intended to erect an impassable protective wall around the purity of the Jewish family.
Laws of Marriage and the Prevention of Iggun in the Case of a Husband Unable to Consummate
A further intricate issue that displays Rabbi Avraham's sensitivity to the status of women and to the prevention of iggun (the plight of the "chained" wife) concerns an unmarried man who marries a woman and it turns out that he cannot consummate the marriage with her because of impotence, when the husband claims that a spell was cast on him ("they bound me") and asks to test himself with another woman [cite: 17]. The wife, on the other hand, refuses to wait and demands her divorce [cite: 17].
Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki ruled that the wife is not obliged to wait for the husband's attempts, and that she is entitled to leave him with a get immediately, receiving her full ketubah, the supplement to the ketubah and the dowry she brought with her from her father's house [cite: 17]. He reasoned that since she had given herself to the marriage and he is unable to realize it, the matter becomes as though he does not want his wife, and she should not be punished with iggun or with monetary loss because of his personal failings [cite: 17].
Systematic Use of the Rules of "Kim Li" According to the View of the Ritzba in Monetary Law
In the responsa "Zera Avraham" (simanim 11–12), Rabbi Avraham deals with the legal rules of Choshen Mishpat, foremost among them the plea of "kim li" (the defendant's plea that he holds a particular halakhic opinion that exempts him from payment) [cite: 17]. He ruled that in places where the courts were accustomed to accept the plea of "kim li," the defendant may plead "kim li" according to the view of the Ritzba (Rabbi Yitzchak ben Asher HaLevi), even though this view remained in doubt in the Gemara and concerns the efficacy of seizing property [cite: 17]. This determination shows his readiness to give great halakhic weight to local legal custom and to the ability of the possessor to protect his property against claims by relying on minority opinions of the great Rishonim, while expanding the legal means of defense in the court [cite: 17].
Immediate Loss of the Ketubah When Divorce Is Compelled on the Plea of "Ma'is Alai"
In cases in which the wife demands a divorce on the plea of "ma'is alai" (when the husband is repulsive to her and she is unable to live with him), Rabbi Avraham Yitzchaki ruled that if the court sees fit to compel the husband to divorce, the wife forfeits her ketubah immediately [cite: 18]. This ruling reflects balanced legal thinking; on the one hand it allows the release of the wife from the shackles of an unbearable marriage by means of the mechanism of compulsion, but on the other hand it protects the husband against the monetary exploitation of the ground of repulsion, and thereby it balances the rights of both parties when the family unit is dissolved [cite: 18].
The Laws of Blessings over Enjoyment and the Scope of Mutual Responsibility
In the laws of blessings (Orach Chaim, siman 12), Rabbi Avraham addresses the clarification of the foundations of the laws of mutual responsibility (arevut) in blessings [cite: 19]. He discusses the halakhic rule according to which, in blessings over enjoyment (such as the blessing over bread and wine), a person who has already fulfilled his obligation cannot recite the blessing for others in order to discharge their obligation, unlike blessings over commandments, in which "all Israel are responsible for one another" [cite: 19]. These discussions served as a foundation for later rulings concerning the obligation of the blessing ha-motzi over bread at obligatory meals of a commandment, such as on the first night of the festival of Sukkot, even for someone who is not himself eating at that time [cite: 19].
Summary and Historical Conclusions
Historical and bibliographical research on the figure of the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Avraham ben David Yitzchaki reveals a multidimensional leader who acted at a critical crossroads in the history of the Jewry of the Ottoman Empire and of the Land of Israel at the end of the seventeenth century and the beginning of the eighteenth century [cite: 1, 2, 7]. His figure represents a unique synthesis of traditional Sephardi scholarship with uncompromising halakhic and public zeal, intended to preserve the walls of Jewish tradition against the destruction of Sabbateanism [cite: 1, 8].
His work as Rishon LeZion, together with his flight to Hebron and his early resignation, reveals the depth of the economic and political crisis experienced by the Jewish community under the Ottoman rule of bribery and exploitation [cite: 1, 2, 3, 7]. His surprising retirement was not a disengagement from the public, but a direct result of persecution by the authorities, which prevented him from managing the affairs of the community freely from Jerusalem [cite: 7]. On the other hand, his mission as a shadar was not only a financial enterprise but the transformation of the network of emissaries into an anti-Sabbatean ideological confederation, by means of which he succeeded in harnessing the communities of Izmir, Salonika and Amsterdam to a unified campaign that brought about the denunciation of Nehemiah Hayun and his books [cite: 1, 8].
On the halakhic plane, his book "Zera Avraham" and his original rulings, such as defining the prohibition of seclusion as "be killed rather than transgress" and preventing the iggun of women in cases of serious marital failure, show that Rabbi Avraham did not shrink from adopting stringent or innovative positions when he identified a spiritual or human need of the hour [cite: 15, 16, 17, 18]. These rulings of his remained controversial but were studied in depth by the great decisors of later generations. His literary legacy, as described by his great-grandson the Chida, has remained a monument to the breadth of his knowledge in the revealed and the hidden Torah, and establishes his standing as one of the most influential spiritual and public leaders of the Land of Israel in the early modern period [cite: 1, 4, 5].
